conversation_lines.text: All good. My sisters helped me unpack. I took my morning insulin already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Wonderful. We’re glad to hear it. Call us anytime.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Stay healthy.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last message: your case manager will call this week to check on your transition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll be here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. We’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a reminder to keep your follow-up appointments with neurology and transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have them on my calendar.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. Keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final note: your urine and blood cultures were negative. No infection found.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I was worried about that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No need. You’re on the right track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll close your chart now. Call us if you need anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Ms. ___? I'm Dr. Lee, one of the hospitalists. You've been admitted because your kidney function came back quite high—your creatinine is 4.4, which is more than double your usual baseline.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh… I didn’t know it was that bad. I’ve just been feeling more tired and thirsty lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that makes sense. We also noticed you’ve had some trouble taking your medications regularly. There was an incident where your niece found you unresponsive at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I… I just forgot. I didn’t mean to. I get confused sometimes. I thought I took them.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. It’s not about blame—it’s about keeping you safe. Missing medications, especially with your transplant and diabetes, can really affect your kidneys.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. I try. But I don’t cook much anymore. I just don’t feel like eating.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s something we’re very concerned about. You’re quite thin, and your labs show poor nutrition. We’ve asked nutrition to see you and add supplements to your meals.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t have much appetite. Even water tastes bad sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve also asked psychiatry to evaluate you. Sometimes low mood can affect how we eat and care for ourselves. They think starting a new medication might help with both your appetite and mood.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m not depressed. I’m just tired.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s okay. The medication they’re suggesting—mirtazapine—can help with both. We’ll start it at a low dose and slowly increase it. It might also help you sleep better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it make me gain weight? I don’t want that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might, but in your case, that’s actually a good thing. You need to regain some strength. We’re also stopping Megace because it can increase clot risk and hasn’t been helping much.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay… I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs from last night show your kidney function is already improving—creatinine down to 3.8. We’re giving you IV fluids to help with dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, very good. It means our plan is working. We’re also adjusting your blood pressure meds. Your pressures were high—up to 180—so we’ve added amlodipine and increased your metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been dizzy sometimes. Is that from the pills?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. We’ve stopped furosemide—that’s a water pill—because it can worsen kidney function and increase fall risk. That might help with the dizziness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do fall sometimes. I can’t see well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noticed that. Your glaucoma needs follow-up. You should see an eye doctor soon for new glasses. Poor vision can make it hard to read medication labels.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I can’t even see the numbers on my insulin pen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s exactly why we’re arranging help. A home health aide will come to assist you with meds. Occupational therapy will also visit to see how you’re managing at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want strangers in my house.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. But this is for your safety. You were found unresponsive once—we don’t want that to happen again. This way, someone can make sure you’re eating and taking your pills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: …Okay. If it keeps me out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your tremor seems worse. Is it bothering you more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially when I try to eat or write. I thought it was from the tacrolimus.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your level—it’s stable. So it’s likely your essential tremor progressing. We’ll recommend a neurology follow-up, but we won’t change anything now unless it worsens.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it get worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It can, but we’ll monitor it. For now, the priority is your kidneys and nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray yesterday. It shows your lungs are clear—no pneumonia. The old changes are healing, so no antibiotics needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had a cough. I’m glad it’s not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, but we did notice something else—swollen lymph nodes near your collarbone. It’s new. We’re concerned it could be something serious, like cancer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Cancer? But I had liver cancer years ago…

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Because of your history, we want to check this. Once your kidneys improve, you’ll need a CT scan to see what’s going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I need another biopsy?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly, but we’ll wait for the scan first. No need to worry yet, but we can’t ignore it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great news—your creatinine is now 2.9, and today’s labs show it’s trending down to 2.7. Your kidneys are recovering well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. Does that mean I can go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Almost. We’re finalizing your discharge plan. You’ll go home with a nurse and aide to help with meds. You’ll also keep seeing PACT and OT.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin? I was on 10 units twice a day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve lowered it to 6 units twice a day. Your sugars were too low at times. We also adjusted your sliding scale. Your diabetes team will follow up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I don’t want another episode like last time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: This plan should help. And with the home support, you’ll be safer. We’re also switching from citalopram to mirtazapine—remember, it helps with mood and appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll take it as prescribed, I promise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Last day! Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 2.7, sugars are in range, and you’ve been eating better with the supplements.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Discharge is tomorrow. Keep drinking at least two liters of water daily. Follow up with nephrology, psychiatry, eye doctor, and your transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll write it down. With help, I think I can manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning! You’re cleared to go home. Your nurse will review all your meds and instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m ready. I’ll do better this time.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re here to support you. Call if anything feels off. Take care, Ms. ___.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You came in today after a liver biopsy and ultrasound, correct?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. The ultrasound showed something about my liver artery being narrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the ultrasound suggested possible narrowing in the main hepatic artery. That’s why we’re keeping you overnight—to give you IV fluids and do a CT scan tomorrow to get a clearer picture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. Is that serious? I feel fine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s reassuring. You’re not having any pain or nausea, which is good. The narrowing could affect blood flow, so we want to check it carefully with the CT scan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the biopsy? Was that for my liver enzymes going up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Your alkaline phosphatase and transaminases have been slowly rising. The biopsy will help us see if there’s any sign of rejection or other liver issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had rejection before, years ago. But my last biopsy was normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your history shows that. We’ll follow up on the biopsy results when they come back, but for now, we’re focused on the blood vessel concern.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my other medicines—am I still taking them?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Most of them, yes. We held your lisinopril today because of the CT scan with contrast. You can restart it the day after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, right. I forgot about that. My blood pressure’s usually okay with amlodipine and metoprolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’re continuing those. Your BP has been stable—148 over 85 earlier, which is good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. And my insulin? I had a low sugar episode last week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re monitoring that. You had a mild low during your stay—treated with juice and crackers. You can keep your current insulin doses at home, but we may adjust the glargine next time if needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I get confused with the doses sometimes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We noted that. Elder Affairs has been contacted to help assess your home safety and medication management. They’ll follow up after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. I live alone, but I usually manage.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just want to make sure you have the support you need. It’s important with all your medications and conditions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I understand. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your CT scan results are back. The good news is there’s no narrowing in your hepatic artery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s a relief! So the ultrasound was wrong?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not exactly. The ultrasound showed delayed blood flow, which can suggest narrowing. But the CT scan, which is more detailed, shows the artery is open.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. Anything else from the scan?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. There’s a small new blood clot in a tiny branch of the portal vein in your liver—segment 6. It’s small, so we’re not starting blood thinners.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: A clot? Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s small and not blocking major flow. We’ll monitor it with your liver specialist. It may be related to your history of portal vein issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had the balloon dilation a while back. The main narrowing is better, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, the scan shows the main portal vein narrowing has improved since your angioplasty. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. So what’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll discharge you today. You’ll follow up with your transplant team for the biopsy results and to monitor the small clot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my other doctors? Eye, bones, stomach?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep seeing them. We recommend restarting calcium and vitamin D for your osteopenia—discuss that with your doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t taken those in a while. My appetite’s better since I started mirtazapine.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’re continuing mirtazapine for both your depression and appetite. Keep using your latanoprost drops for glaucoma too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I do. And Keppra for my seizures—still twice a day?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, 500 mg twice daily. No changes there. All your other meds stay the same, including tacrolimus for your transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I can restart lisinopril tomorrow?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, tomorrow morning. We’ll send all this in your discharge instructions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better knowing the artery isn’t blocked.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Just keep all your appointments, especially with your liver team. We’ll make sure they get the results.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check before discharge. You’re feeling well, no pain, no dizziness?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I feel fine. Ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Nurse will go over your discharge papers, and you should be out within the hour.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One last thing—your HCV viral load is still high, but you’re not on treatment now. Your transplant team will decide if that needs to change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I know. They’ve held off because of my other health issues.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we’ll continue monitoring. Take care, and call if you have any concerns.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee. I’ll be taking care of you during your stay. Can you tell me what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been feeling weak and not eating much. I’ve had diarrhea for about two weeks now, and I’ve lost weight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your primary doctor mentioned your kidney numbers were high and you were dehydrated. You’ve also lost about 10 pounds recently?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I haven’t had much appetite. I feel cold all the time and just tired. I haven’t been urinating much either.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Dehydration can affect your kidneys. We’ve started you on IV fluids to help with that. Your creatinine was high at 3.6, but it’s already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? My kidneys have always been a little off since the transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s an acute issue on top of your chronic kidney disease. We think it’s due to the diarrhea and not drinking enough. With fluids, it’s improving. We’ll keep monitoring it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that’s a relief. What about the diarrhea? It’s been watery and constant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We tested your stool. It’s not C. diff or a common bacterial infection. We’re still waiting on some viral and parasite tests, but no treatment is needed right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had C. diff before. I was worried it came back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No, it’s not C. diff this time. Your immune system is suppressed, so we have to be careful, but so far nothing dangerous shows up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve also been feeling shaky and unsteady, like I’m walking drunk.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from your essential tremor or maybe weakness from not eating. We’ll check your electrolytes and make sure nothing else is going on.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I take Prograf for my liver. Could that be off?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good point. Your level came back high—12.6, which is above the usual range. That’s likely because of the diarrhea affecting absorption. We’ll lower your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help me feel better?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It should. High levels can cause tremors and confusion. We’re reducing it to 1 mg twice a day. You’ll need to check the level again tomorrow morning before your dose.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll do that. What about my liver? I still have hepatitis C.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your viral load is still high, but your liver doctors think we can consider treatment now since your kidney function is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I didn’t take it before because my kidneys were too weak.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Now that your creatinine is coming down, it might be safe. We’ll discuss it with your liver team after discharge.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That sounds good. I’ve been so down lately. I don’t enjoy eating or doing anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand. You’re on mirtazapine, which helps with both appetite and mood. We’ll keep that going. Depression is common with chronic illness.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I’ve also been coughing a little, but no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray. It shows some old scarring in your lung, but no pneumonia. Your heart size is normal too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I traveled for my niece’s funeral recently. I thought maybe I caught something.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of infection now. The cough might just be from dry air or irritation. Keep an eye on it, but I’m not worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are improving. Creatinine is down to 1.5, and your acid levels are normalizing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! Is the diarrhea gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it resolved yesterday. That’s a big reason your kidneys are recovering. We’ll keep you on fluids today and see how you do.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m feeling a bit stronger. Can I eat something light?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, start with small amounts—broth, toast. Your stomach has been through a lot. We’ll advance as tolerated.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your urine culture showed E. coli, but since you have no symptoms of a UTI, we won’t treat it. It’s likely from old infections.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve had UTIs before. Should I be concerned?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. You’re not running a fever or having pain. We’ll watch it, but no antibiotics are needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV and other virus tests came back negative. No parasites either. That’s good news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So nothing serious is causing the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not that we can find. It may have just been from a mild virus or your medications. Since it’s resolved, we’ll focus on recovery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re doing well. Your labs are stable, and you’re eating and drinking. We’re planning to discharge you today.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. What do I need to do after I go home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: First, check your tacrolimus level tomorrow morning before your dose. Call your liver doctor with the result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember. And keep drinking fluids?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Stay hydrated, eat small meals, and take your medications as adjusted. Follow up with your liver clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will I start hepatitis C treatment?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver team will decide, but now that your kidneys are better, it’s a real option. They’ll contact you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. We’re glad to see you improving. Take care, and don’t hesitate to call if anything changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Of course. The nurse will go over your discharge instructions and medications before you leave.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’ll make sure to read them carefully.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during your stay. You were admitted because of diarrhea and dehydration. How have you been feeling?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve had diarrhea for about three weeks now. Every time I eat, I need to go. It’s loose and has mucus, but no blood. I feel bloated, but no pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. And you’ve been eating and drinking normally otherwise?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Not really. I haven’t had much appetite. I’ve been sipping water, but not a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Your labs show your kidney function is worse than usual—creatinine is 2.2, up from your baseline of 1.6 to 2.0. This is likely due to dehydration from the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, that’s not good. My liver clinic said my Prograf level was high too. Should I stop it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your tacrolimus level—it was 5.6, which is a bit high. We’ll hold one dose and restart at the same 1 mg twice daily. We’ll monitor it closely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Could the diarrhea be from the Prograf?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s possible. Tacrolimus can cause diarrhea, especially in transplant patients. But we also need to rule out infections, so we sent stool tests.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I had those at the clinic. They said no C. diff or common bacteria.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, and we also tested for parasites like Giardia and Cryptosporidium. Those came back negative. We have two more stool tests pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I haven’t had fevers or chills. Do you think it’s just from the meds?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Possibly. Since you’re not running a fever and the tests are negative, it may be related to tacrolimus or just a mild gastroenteritis. We’ll keep an eye on it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did an abdominal X-ray to check for any blockage. It showed a normal bowel gas pattern—no obstruction or swelling.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. My stomach still feels full, but not painful.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, bloating can happen with frequent bowel movements. The good news is your diarrhea has improved since you’ve been here.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve only gone once today. That’s a big change.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great progress. We’ve been giving you IV fluids and albumin to help your kidneys. Your creatinine is already coming down.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel a bit more energy. But my blood counts—are they okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white blood cell count and hemoglobin dropped a little—from 3.4 to 2.0 and 10.3 to 9.0. But we think it’s due to dilution from the fluids, not a new problem.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection or bleeding?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: No signs of either. All your cell lines are down equally, which supports the dilution idea. We’ll check again before you go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your latest labs show your kidney function is improving—creatinine is now 1.5. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great! What about my other meds? I usually take Lasix and nadolol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We held your Lasix because of dehydration. We also paused nadolol temporarily due to the kidney issue, but we’ve restarted it since your blood pressure is stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. Should I restart Lasix at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not yet. You should follow up with your liver doctor first. They’ll decide when it’s safe to restart based on your fluid status.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your diarrhea has completely stopped, and your creatinine is now 1.2—back to your normal range.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful! So I can go home soon?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, likely tomorrow. Your tacrolimus level is now 3.8, which is in the target range, so we’ll keep your dose at 1 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the pending stool tests?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One is still pending, but the others were negative for parasites. You should follow up with hepatology to get the final result.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. What about my blood counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still low, but we still believe it’s from the fluid expansion. Your doctor will repeat the CBC as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re cleared to go home today. Your labs are stable, and you’ve had no diarrhea for two days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. What should I do at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Stay well hydrated. Continue all your usual meds except Lasix—you’ll need to see your liver doctor before restarting it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the tacrolimus?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Keep taking 1 mg twice daily. Your level is stable, but your doctor will monitor it closely, especially with your kidney changes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to follow up. Thank you for taking care of me.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Call if you have any concerns—especially if diarrhea returns or you feel dehydrated. Take care!

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be part of your care team. You were admitted because your liver tests were elevated, and we’re concerned about possible rejection of your transplant. Do you have any questions so far?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I’ve been feeling fine. No pain or fever. Why would rejection happen now?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a great question. Rejection can happen even without symptoms. Your ALT and AST were high a few days ago, though they’ve improved a bit. We’ll do a liver ultrasound and likely a biopsy to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember the ultrasound. It showed ascites and normal blood vessels, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. The ultrasound showed your liver blood vessels are open, no blockages, but there is moderate fluid in your belly—ascites. That’s common with liver disease. We’ll check the fluid to make sure it’s not infected.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We did a paracentesis yesterday—drained some fluid from your abdomen. The lab says no infection, which is great news.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. But what about the liver test? Is it rejection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re still waiting on the biopsy, which is scheduled for today. But your HCV and CMV tests came back negative, so it’s not a viral flare-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my urine test showed bacteria—should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we found Klebsiella and Citrobacter in your urine. It’s a urinary tract infection. We’ll start antibiotics to treat it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We just got back from your liver biopsy. It showed signs of acute rejection—your immune system is attacking the new liver.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh no. Is that serious?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s treatable. We’re starting you on high-dose IV steroids—methylprednisolone—for five days. We’ll also increase your tacrolimus and add a new medication called mycophenolate.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will the steroids make my blood sugar worse? I’m diabetic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, steroids can raise blood sugar. We’ve started an insulin drip to manage it and will switch you to a new insulin regimen soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are starting to come down. That’s a good sign the treatment is working.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. But I feel a bit more tired, and my legs are still a little swollen.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The swelling is from the ascites and low protein. We’re holding your Lasix for now because your kidney function is a little off.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My creatinine is up again, isn’t it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s 1.8 now, up from your baseline. It’s likely due to the higher tacrolimus dose and the steroids. We’re watching it closely and adjusting meds accordingly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re continuing the steroids. Your tacrolimus level is now 7.8, which is in the target range. That’s good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the new meds—mycophenolate and prednisone—will I stay on those?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you’ll go home on prednisone 40 mg daily and mycophenolate twice a day. The prednisone will be tapered slowly after your transplant follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your blood sugar has been high, but we’ve adjusted your insulin. You’ll go home on glargine 8 units twice daily and a sliding scale.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll need to check it more often, I guess.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, especially while on steroids. Call your doctor if it’s over 300 or under 70 regularly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We did a chest X-ray today—no pneumonia. Your lungs look stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I haven’t had any cough or shortness of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are still coming down, but not as fast as we’d like. We’re thinking about repeating the biopsy to see if the rejection is improving.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Another biopsy? Is it safe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very safe with ultrasound guidance. We need to make sure the treatment is working and if we need to adjust anything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The repeat biopsy shows the inflammation is better, but there’s still some cholangitis—bile duct inflammation. We’ll keep you on the current treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So the steroids are helping?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, definitely. The rejection signs are improving. We’ll keep monitoring your labs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your kidney function is still a concern. Creatinine is 1.8. We’re keeping Lasix stopped for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood pressure is up—should I restart my nadolol?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ve switched you to carvedilol instead. It helps with both blood pressure and protects your varices, and it’s safer with your current kidney function.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Another chest X-ray today—your left pleural effusion has improved. Lungs look clear.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I feel like I can breathe better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re planning a therapeutic paracentesis tomorrow to remove more fluid. You’ve been feeling bloated, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my belly feels tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Removing the fluid should help. We’ll check the new fluid to make sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The paracentesis went well. We removed 2.5 liters. The fluid looks clean—no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel less pressure. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your liver enzymes are stable, and you’re off the insulin drip. We’re finalizing your discharge plan.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good news—you’re being discharged today. Your rejection is responding to treatment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll take tacrolimus 4 mg twice daily, mycophenolate twice daily, and prednisone 40 mg daily. Keep taking your Keppra, amlodipine, and the new carvedilol.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Glargine 8 units twice daily and a sliding scale. Your dose will likely go down once steroids are tapered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: What about the primidone? I noticed it was lowered.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we reduced it to 25 mg daily because of interactions with your liver meds. Don’t increase it without talking to your liver doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Got it. And when do I follow up?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You need labs next week—CBC, liver tests, INR, and tacrolimus level. Fax them to your transplant team. And see your hepatologist soon to discuss tapering steroids and restarting Lasix.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the UTI—is it gone?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, you completed the antibiotics. No further treatment is needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad this is behind me. Thank you for explaining everything.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You did great. Keep monitoring your blood sugar, take your meds, and call if you feel worse. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thanks again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better already.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s the goal. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. See you at follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll see how you’re doing then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for all your help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome. Stay well.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take your time getting ready. We’ll have your discharge papers soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I’m just gathering my things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Nurse will be in with your prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Great, thanks.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Me too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Have a good day.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: You too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll be in touch with your outpatient team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, good.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set. Nurse will assist you shortly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re very welcome.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I'm Dr. Lee, one of your hospital doctors. I understand you've been feeling unwell—can you tell me more about what’s been going on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, yes. I’ve just been so tired lately, and I’ve lost my appetite. I’ve been losing weight—down to about 51 kilograms. I’ve also had diarrhea, about 4 or 5 times a day, watery, for about a week now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Any fevers, chills, nausea, or vomiting?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No fevers or chills. No nausea or vomiting. My ascites hasn’t changed, and I’m not short of breath.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Thanks. We’ll run some tests to check for infection and see why you’re having diarrhea. Your blood work shows low white blood cells and low bicarbonate, which may explain your fatigue. Your kidney function is also a bit worse than usual.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that from the diarrhea? I’ve been drinking fluids, but maybe not enough.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s likely part of it—dehydration from diarrhea can affect your kidneys and acid levels. We’ll give you IV fluids and sodium bicarbonate to help correct that.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative for C. diff, Salmonella, Shigella, and other infections. Blood cultures are also negative so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection? What else could it be?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re considering that one of your medications—mycophenolate—might be causing the diarrhea. It’s rare, but it can lead to something called ischemic colitis. We’d like to do an endoscopy to check.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: An endoscopy? Is that safe with my low white blood cells?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, we’ll take precautions. It’s important to find the cause. We’ll also check your varices since it’s been a while.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your CMV test came back negative, which is good. No sign of CMV colitis. But we still want to proceed with the endoscopy tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes me feel better. And my white blood cells—are they improving?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’re still low—your absolute neutrophil count is 435. We think this is from your immunosuppressants. We’ve slightly lowered your tacrolimus and mycophenolate doses to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that affect my transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re balancing risks. The lower counts increase infection risk, but we’re monitoring closely. Your liver enzymes are stable, so rejection isn’t a concern right now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We got your endoscopy results. The stomach and duodenum look normal. In the colon, the biopsies show signs of ischemic colitis—reduced blood flow to the bowel.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that serious? What causes that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s mild, and we believe it’s related to mycophenolate. That’s why you’ve had diarrhea. We’re switching you to a different form—myfortic—which may be easier on your gut.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will that help the diarrhea?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We expect it will. Many patients improve quickly after the switch.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You had a chest X-ray last night because your white count dropped and you had a slight fever. It showed some atelectasis—collapsed lung areas—but no pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been coughing a little. Should I be worried?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not at this point. It’s likely from not taking deep breaths due to feeling weak. We’ll encourage you to use the incentive spirometer to help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your diarrhea has improved since switching to myfortic. That’s a good sign.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, only 1 or 2 times a day now, and more formed. I feel a bit more energy too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Great. Your kidney function is also improving—creatinine down to 1.8. We’ll restart your Bactrim today since it’s safe now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember last time it affected my kidneys. Are you sure it’s okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. The benefit of preventing infections outweighs the risk now that your kidneys are stable.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We checked your zinc level because you mentioned taste changes. It’s low—50, when it should be over 60. We’re starting zinc supplements for 14 days.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. Food hasn’t tasted right. Will zinc help me eat more?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It might. We’re also starting megace to boost your appetite. It can raise blood sugar, so we’ve increased your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ve been having highs and lows. Is that from the megace?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it can cause hyperglycemia. We’ll monitor your sugars closely and adjust insulin as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your white count is slowly improving—ANC now 600. Still low, but trending up. We’ve kept your myfortic dose and tacrolimus at 3 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe to go home with low white counts?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, as long as you watch for fever, cough, or any signs of infection. You’ll need weekly CMV blood tests since we stopped valganciclovir.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember—because I’m at risk for CMV?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. If CMV comes back, we’ll restart treatment. But so far, no sign of it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your liver enzymes are slightly elevated—ALT 65—but stable. We’re not doing a biopsy because of your low counts and no signs of rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not rejection?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not likely. It could be from the medications. We’ll follow it in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve gained about 2 kilograms—up to 53 kg. That’s excellent progress.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m eating more, thanks to megace. My tremor’s a bit worse though.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be from the higher tacrolimus level. We’ll watch it. Don’t stop your primidone.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show creatinine 1.5, bicarbonate 19, and WBC 1.9. All improving. We’re planning for discharge tomorrow if all stays on track.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good news. What will my meds be at home?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll stay on prednisone 10 mg daily, tacrolimus 3 mg twice daily, myfortic 180 mg twice daily, and continue megace for appetite.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my insulin?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, glargine increased to 12 units twice daily, plus sliding scale. We’ll need your PCP to check sugars and kidney function soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: One more thing—we increased your carvedilol to 25 mg twice daily for blood pressure and variceal protection. It’s well tolerated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no dizziness. My last EGD showed only grade I varices, right?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Correct, and no bleeding. That’s a good sign. We’ll repeat EGD in 6 months.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: All set for discharge tomorrow. You’re up to 54.9 kg, kidneys and liver stable, and diarrhea resolved.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m glad. I’ll be careful about infections, check my sugars, and come to all my appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. Call us if you develop fever, persistent diarrhea, or confusion. Your niece is listed as contact—she’ll help?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, she’ll pick me up and help at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Final labs look good. WBC still low at 1.9, but stable. Continue weekly CMV testing. We’ll see you in transplant clinic in one week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you for explaining everything. I feel much better than when I came in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve done really well. Keep up the good work with diet, meds, and follow-up.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Time to go home. Here’s your discharge summary and prescriptions. Remember: watch for fever, check blood sugars, and keep all appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you, Dr. Lee. I appreciate all your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care, and we’ll see you soon in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure to bring someone with me to the appointments.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good idea. Especially for the first few visits while you’re adjusting.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And I’ll keep using the incentive spirometer at home to help my lungs.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Excellent. That will help prevent complications. You’re doing all the right things.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I want to stay healthy for my family.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And you’re on the right path. Keep in touch with the team—we’re here for you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. Have a safe trip home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Goodbye for now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye. We’ll see you in clinic.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll be there.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: And remember—call if anything changes before then.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I feel strong enough to go home now.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ve made great progress. Proud of how far you’ve come.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I couldn’t have done it without your team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re glad we could help. Now go home and rest.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Take care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You too. See you soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Bye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Goodbye.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, I’m Dr. Lee. I’ll be your doctor during this stay. You were admitted because your kidney function was worsening. Can you tell me how you’ve been feeling since your last discharge?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Hi, Doctor. I’ve been tired and weak, same as before. But my diarrhea came back, even though it had stopped after the last hospitalization.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. Your labs from your doctor’s office showed your creatinine went from 1.5 to 2.1, and your potassium was a bit high. We’re concerned this could be due to dehydration or a medication effect.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Could it be from the Bactrim? I remember they stopped it last time and then restarted it when I left.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s a good point. Bactrim can affect the kidneys, especially in someone with chronic kidney disease. We’ve decided to stop Bactrim for now to see if that helps.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that makes sense. What about the diarrhea? It’s really loose again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re checking your stool for infections. Last time, we thought it might be from Myfortic, which replaced your old immunosuppressant. You were improving, but now it’s back.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So could Myfortic still be causing it even after switching?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s possible. Some patients remain sensitive. If the stool tests are negative for infection, we may need to stop Myfortic completely.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’d rather not stay on something that’s making me sick. But won’t stopping affect my transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep your other anti-rejection meds—tacrolimus and prednisone. They’re still protecting your liver. We’ll monitor closely and adjust as needed.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you. What about my blood counts? They were low last time too.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, your white blood cell count is still low—especially your neutrophils. That’s called neutropenia. It’s likely due to your immunosuppressants, not an infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that dangerous? I don’t want to get sick.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re watching closely. No fever or signs of infection now. We’ve stopped Bactrim and may stop Myfortic—both can contribute. Your counts should improve.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the chest X-ray they did—did it show anything?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It shows some old scarring and atelectasis—collapsed lung tissue—on the left side. Nothing new or concerning for pneumonia.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good to know. I’ve been coughing a little, but no fever.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep an eye on it. For now, we’re giving you IV fluids and albumin to support your kidneys and help with any dehydration.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your stool tests came back negative—no C. diff, salmonella, or other infections. That supports our thought that the diarrhea is medication-related.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So it’s not an infection. That’s a relief. What’s next?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re going to stop Myfortic completely. We’ll rely on tacrolimus and prednisone for immunosuppression. We hope this stops the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And my blood counts? Any change?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Still low, but stable. We also checked your CMV viral load—it’s undetectable, which is good. That means CMV isn’t causing the low counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I remember they stopped valcyte last time. Should I restart it?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not right now. Since CMV is not detected and you’re not on valcyte, we’ll continue to monitor weekly as an outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. And my kidneys—any improvement?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your creatinine is starting to come down—from 2.2 to 1.9. That’s a good sign. We’ll keep encouraging fluids and good nutrition.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning show continued improvement. Creatinine is now 1.6, and your potassium is normal. The albumin and stopping Bactrim are helping.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. My diarrhea has slowed down too—only once this morning and less watery.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s excellent. Stopping Myfortic seems to be working. Your white count is still low but trending up—neutrophils from 0.59 to 0.89.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So I’m on the right track?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. We’re also continuing your Megace for appetite and Nepro with meals to help with nutrition. You’ve gained a little weight since last admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel stronger. But I’m worried about going home with low blood counts.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll set up weekly blood tests with your PCP. If anything changes, you’ll know quickly. And you can always come back if you feel unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I appreciate that. I don’t want to keep coming back, but I know I need to stay on top of this.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We consulted palliative care to help discuss your goals. You mentioned you’d want to return if needed—that’s perfectly okay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, I want to stay healthy and at home, but I’ll come back if I need to. My niece helps me a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s good support. We’ll make sure she’s in the loop. Now, your liver enzymes are stable, and your tremor is still there but not worsening.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: It’s from the tacrolimus, right? I’ve had it for years.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s common. We checked your tacrolimus level—it’s 9.0, which is in the target range. We’ll keep it at 3 mg twice daily.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your labs this morning are even better. Creatinine is 1.4, and your neutrophil count is now 0.99—almost normal. You’re ready to go home tomorrow.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s wonderful. What meds will I be on?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll continue tacrolimus, prednisone, carvedilol, amlodipine, insulin, and your other usual meds. But Myfortic and Bactrim are stopped.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And Megace and Nepro?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, keep those. Also continue lactulose and rifaximin for liver health, and sodium bicarbonate for the mild acidosis.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’ll make sure I have all the prescriptions.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll send them to your pharmacy. Follow up with your PCP in a few days for labs and with the liver team next week.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And if I feel worse?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Call your doctor or come to the ER if you have fever, severe diarrhea, confusion, or feel generally unwell.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. Thank you for explaining everything so clearly.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your final labs are excellent—creatinine 1.3, neutrophils 0.99. You’re medically ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel ready. I’ve been walking more and eating better.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your physical exam is stable. Lungs are clear, belly soft, no swelling in legs. We’re discharging you with home health for lab draws.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That helps a lot. I’ll follow up with my doctors.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll coordinate with Dr. Chen on the liver team. Keep taking your meds as prescribed and watch for any new symptoms.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. I’m glad we figured out what was causing the diarrhea.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, stopping Myfortic and Bactrim made the difference. Your kidney function and blood counts are on the mend.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I’m hopeful this time I can stay out of the hospital.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We all are. You’re doing well. Take care, and don’t hesitate to reach out.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you, Doctor. I really appreciate your care.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just a quick check-in before discharge. Any last questions?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No, I think I’ve got it all. Meds, follow-up, when to call. I’m ready to go home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Perfect. We’ll have the discharge papers ready soon. Rest well and keep up the good work.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Nurse will be in with your prescriptions and instructions. Safe travels home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you again. I’ll see my doctors soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Take care. We’re here if you need us.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the internal medicine team. I understand you came in with leg cramps and high blood sugar?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, doctor. These leg cramps are terrible—both thighs, calves, even my feet. And my sugar was 500 this morning. I didn’t feel that bad, but the transplant clinic told me to come in.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You’ve had some cramping before, but not this severe?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Just mild calf cramps now and then. But this is different—constant, painful. And I’ve been urinating all night. I thought it was because I’ve been drinking more water in this heat.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That makes sense. High blood sugar can cause increased urination and dehydration, which might explain the cramps. We’ve checked your labs, and your glucose was 339, sodium low at 130, and potassium high at 6.5. Your kidney function is also a bit off—creatinine is 2.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh. Is that serious? I’ve had kidney issues before.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s what we call acute-on-chronic kidney injury. Likely due to dehydration and your diabetes being harder to control, especially since you’re on prednisone for your liver transplant.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, since I started prednisone, my sugars have been all over the place. I’m on 14 units of Lantus twice a day, but I don’t always take the sliding scale insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That could be part of the problem. Prednisone increases blood sugar, and if the insulin isn’t adjusted, it can get out of control. We’re going to start you on IV fluids to help with hydration and correct your electrolytes.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay. But I’m worried—I need to get home. My niece is out of town, and no one’s feeding my dogs or paying my bills.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I understand your concern, but leaving now could be dangerous. Your potassium is high, which can affect your heart, and your sugars need to stabilize. We want to keep you safe.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I guess you’re right. But how long will I be here?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’re hoping just a couple of days. We’ll monitor your labs and adjust your insulin. We also want to check your abdomen—your exam shows some swelling, and we’re concerned about fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my belly has been bigger lately. Is that from the transplant?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It could be ascites—fluid from your liver condition. We’ll do an ultrasound tomorrow to check, and if there’s fluid, we may need to drain a small amount to make sure there’s no infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. The ultrasound confirmed mild ascites. We’d like to do a paracentesis—just a small sample—to rule out infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is it safe? I’ve had procedures before, but I’m nervous.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, it’s very safe. We’ll use ultrasound to guide us, numb the area, and just take a small amount of fluid. You’ll feel pressure, but not pain.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The paracentesis went well. We removed about 800 mL of fluid and sent it for testing. The good news is you’re not showing signs of infection—no white blood cells or bacteria seen so far.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s a relief. What about my sugar and kidneys?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Your glucose is coming down—now 256—and your potassium is normal at 4.4. Creatinine improved to 1.6. So your kidneys are recovering with fluids.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the cramps?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: They’ve resolved, which supports our theory that dehydration and electrolyte shifts were the cause. We gave you albumin to help with fluid balance.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I feel much better. But what about my insulin? I don’t want this happening again.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The endocrine team recommended switching to a premixed insulin—70/30 NPH-humalog. 40 units in the morning, 20 at bedtime. It combines long-acting and short-acting insulin, which may help control both fasting and mealtime sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: And the sliding scale?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’ll still use Humalog as a sliding scale. The key is to check your sugars before meals and at bedtime and call your diabetologist daily until your appointment.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Every day? That’s a lot.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Just for now. It helps him adjust your dose safely. We want to avoid both highs and lows—especially since you’ve had low sugars before, like 44, without feeling it.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that scares me. I didn’t even know I was low.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. So we’ll keep a close eye. Your tacrolimus level was a bit low this morning—5.3—but it was drawn early, so we’ll check again outpatient.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I have a transplant clinic visit coming up. They’ll handle that?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, they’ll review your level and adjust if needed. For now, you’re stable. We’re planning to discharge you tomorrow if your labs stay steady.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: That’s good. I’m feeling much better. Thank you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Morning. Your labs are stable—glucose 256, creatinine 1.6, potassium 4.4. The chest X-ray showed a small pneumonia, but you’re not symptomatic, and it’s likely not related to this admission.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: No cough or fever. Should I be treated?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll monitor. Since you’re not sick, antibiotics aren’t needed now. But mention it to your primary doctor.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re cleared to go home. Continue all your meds, especially the new insulin. Call Dr. ___ daily with your sugar readings. Follow up with your diabetologist and transplant team.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I will. And thank you—for listening and helping me stay.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: You’re welcome. Take care of yourself, and we’ll see you in clinic soon.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Hello, Mrs. ___? I'm Dr. ___ from the medicine team. I understand you were admitted because of worsening swelling in your belly and some trouble with your blood sugars.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, that’s right. My stomach has been getting bigger, and I’ve been feeling short of breath. And my sugars have been all over the place.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: I see. You also mentioned some increased tremors lately?

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Yes, my hands shake more. It’s making it hard to eat or write. I take primidone, but it doesn’t seem to help as much anymore.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll talk to neurology about adjusting your dose. For now, we’ve reviewed your labs. Your blood sugar was 278 when you came in, and your kidney function is a bit worse than before—creatinine is 2.0.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is that bad? It used to be 1.5.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: It’s elevated, likely due to your tacrolimus levels being a bit high in the past. Your current level is 3.2, which is low, so we plan to increase your dose to help prevent rejection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Oh, okay. I’ve been trying to take everything, but sometimes I forget.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We understand. That’s part of why your doctor admitted you—to make sure everything is stable and to help coordinate support at home.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: My sister is coming soon. I think that will help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. We’ll also have social work and occupational therapy help set things up. For now, we ordered a chest X-ray to check your breathing.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Was it okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes, no pneumonia or new fluid. Just a small old scar at the left lung base. Your heart size is normal.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Good. I was worried.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll keep monitoring. Get some rest tonight. I’ll be back tomorrow morning.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. We’re planning a paracentesis today—removing some fluid from your abdomen to help with the swelling and to check for infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Will it hurt?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll use local anesthesia. You might feel pressure, but not sharp pain. It’s ultrasound-guided, so it’s very precise.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, I trust you.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: The procedure went well. We removed 900 mL of fluid—about two pounds. It was straw-colored and cloudy, but no signs of infection.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: I already feel a little better. My belly isn’t so tight.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s great. The fluid showed a white count of 111, which is slightly elevated but not high enough for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis. No bacteria grew in culture.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: So no antibiotics?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Not needed. We’ll keep monitoring. Also, your blood sugars have been running high, so the diabetes team is adjusting your insulin.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Last time I was here, I went from high sugars to low ones after the change. I was scared.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: That’s why we’re making changes slowly. You’re staying on glargine 14 units twice daily, but we’re switching your sliding scale to Novolog for better control.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Okay, that sounds safer.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Yes. And we’ve increased your primidone to 50 mg daily for the tremors. Neurology agrees it should help.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Thank you. I hope it makes a difference.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: We’ll see. Also, we’re stopping the megestrol—Megace. It can cause fluid retention and make ascites worse.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: But I’ve been eating better lately.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Exactly. Since your appetite has improved, we don’t need it. We want to avoid anything that worsens fluid buildup.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Makes sense.

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
conversation_lines.text: Good morning. Your labs are stable. Creatinine is 1.8, glucose is 152 this morning. Tacrolimus level is pending.

conversation_lines.speaker: Patient
conversation_lines.text: Is my liver okay?

conversation_lines.speaker: Doctor
